text: The classification of so-called small-sized wineries is changing - a small-sized winery is defined as a type of wine production facility whose annual production does not exceed 25,000 liters of wine (16.04.2026, 16:24)
The classification of so-called small-scale wineries is changing - a small-scale winery is defined as a type of wine production facility whose annual production does not exceed 25,000 liters of wine.

Furthermore, organoleptic testing becomes mandatory for alcoholic beverages of Protected Designation of Origin produced in Georgia, as well as for all categories of wine intended for export and sale on the local consumer market. This requirement will not apply to wine produced in small-sized wineries.

Relevant changes are being implemented in the Law "On Vine and Wine," which was prepared by the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture. The government submitted the project to the Parliament.

According to the project, the labeling of certified alcoholic beverages intended for sale will be mandatory. The Wine Agency will carry out the labeling in accordance with the rules established by the Minister of Environmental Protection and Agriculture.

Taking into account the current Law on Vine and Wine, a small-scale winery was defined as an entrepreneur who owns a traditional family cellar and whose annual production does not exceed 40,000 liters. With the amendments, this amount is being reduced from 40,000 to 25,000 liters.

"Since the concept of a small-scale winery and excess production have effectively lost their meaning, there is a need to implement changes to this term and reduce the production volume of wine produced in a small-scale winery."

It should be noted that the mentioned wine, through its organoleptic characteristics and taste properties, has an overall impact on the reputation of Georgian wine in both local and international markets. To regulate this very issue, it is important to add a new category—Natural Wine—instead of "house wine," which will not be subject to mandatory organoleptic testing only if it is produced in a small-scale winery and, at the same time, the corresponding mark designated for natural wine is placed on the label, ensuring that consumers are informed in advance about the product itself.

Furthermore, it is important to maintain the quality and reputation of Georgian wine in both local and international markets; accordingly, to ensure the delivery of high-quality products to consumers, it becomes necessary for all categories of wine—both for export and those intended for sale on the local market—to be subject to organoleptic testing.

"Based on the above, for the purpose of regulating the issue and implementing appropriate mechanisms, it is advisable to introduce marking for alcoholic beverages and expand the scope of organoleptic testing," explains the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture in the explanatory note attached to the draft law.
